prompt.context: Our client is a private equity firm interested in acquiring PlasticWorld, a plastic packaging manufacturer. PlasticWorld makes plastic packaging for beverages, cosmetics, household and automotive chemicals. The products are top quality — the company has 350 sets of molds with different materials, finishes, and colors, and is constantly innovating. The overall product mix has not changed in recent years. The sales force is considered 'the best in breed' and the company has been holding its market share. Two years ago PlasticWorld invested further in equipment for product innovation. PlasticWorld's customers exhibit strong loyalty and are experiencing increasing pressures in their industries to innovate plastic packaging.
prompt.question: PlasticWorld's owners are requesting $25M. The offer is final. Should our client buy?

clarifying_info.q: How is the sales force compensated?
clarifying_info.a: The sales force is compensated based on market share.

clarifying_info.q: Are prices dropping because of competition or a need to compete on price?
clarifying_info.a: Products are top quality and customers are loyal; most would buy even at a higher price. The drop in prices is not driven by competitive pressure.

clarifying_info.q: Is the profitability drop an industry-wide trend?
clarifying_info.a: You would need to look at competitor data — request Exhibit 2 if you want to explore this.

clarifying_info.q: What drove the increase in depreciation?
clarifying_info.a: Two years ago, PlasticWorld invested in new equipment for product innovation, which caused the depreciation to rise.

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld P&L Statement in the Past Three Years
exhibits.shows: A three-year income statement (2007–2009) for PlasticWorld showing Sales ($), Volume (units), COGS ($), SG&A ($), Depreciation ($), and EBIT ($).

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld and Industry Peers Profit Margins
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing profit margins (%) for PlasticWorld and six competitors (Competitor A through F).
exhibits.data: Competitors A–F all show positive profit margins roughly in the 5–12% range; PlasticWorld shows a negative profit margin of approximately –6%.

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld Valuation by Profit Margin
exhibits.shows: A sensitivity analysis curve showing company valuation ($M) as a function of profit margin (%). The x-axis runs from –10% to +15% profit margin; the y-axis runs from 0 to ~50 $M.
exhibits.data: At 0% profit margin the company valuation is approximately $25M; at the industry-average profit margin (~10%) the valuation reaches approximately $40M.

framework: Company value assessment: determine current valuation and required margin to justify $25M asking price
Revenue trend analysis: diagnose why revenues are falling despite growing sales volume (pricing vs. volume vs. mix)
Cost structure review: examine COGS, SG&A, and depreciation trajectory
Benchmark vs. industry: compare PlasticWorld profitability to competitors to determine if the problem is systemic or company-specific
Profit improvement levers: identify feasible changes to bring margin from –6% to 0% (break-even) and beyond
Deal recommendation: assess whether the $25M price is justified given the value-creation path

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the 2009 profit margin and explain what is driving the financial performance trend.
questions.guidance: Profit margin = EBIT / Sales = –1,176,000 / 18,824,000 ≈ –6%. Sales volume is growing (32.75M → 36.2M units) while revenues are declining ($19.65M → $18.82M), indicating prices per unit are falling. Product mix is unchanged, so pricing is the driver. Depreciation jumped in 2008 from $2.25M to $3.45M due to the equipment investment. Strong candidate independently flags that if volume is growing but revenues are dropping, revenue per unit must be decreasing.

math.setup: Profit margin = EBIT / Revenue; Revenue per unit = Revenue / Volume
math.answer: Profit margin is approximately –6%; revenue per unit has dropped ~13% while volume grew ~10.5%, implying significant price deterioration as the root cause.

questions.prompt: What is the root cause of the price decline? What organizational or structural factor explains why prices are falling despite high product quality and loyal customers?
questions.guidance: The sales force is compensated based on market share, not profitability. This incentivizes salespeople to cut prices to win or retain volume, even when customers would pay more. Since product quality is high and customers are loyal, the price cuts are unnecessary — they are an artifact of the incentive structure. A strong candidate asks about sales force compensation independently.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, is the profitability problem specific to PlasticWorld or industry-wide?
questions.guidance: All six competitors (A–F) show positive profit margins in the ~5–12% range. PlasticWorld is the only entity with a negative margin (~–6%). This confirms the problem is company-specific, not a result of industry headwinds. The candidate should use this to set a realistic profit margin target for improvement.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, at what profit margin is PlasticWorld worth exactly $25M? If the margin reached the industry average (~10%), what would the company be worth?
questions.guidance: At 0% profit margin the sensitivity curve shows a valuation of approximately $25M — exactly the asking price. At the industry-average margin of ~10%, the valuation reaches approximately $40M. Therefore the acquisition is worth making if the PE firm can execute the margin improvement from –6% to 0% (break-even) to justify the price, with meaningful upside toward $40M if industry-average margins are achieved.

math.setup: Read directly from Exhibit 3 valuation sensitivity curve
steps: At profit margin = 0%: company value ≈ $25M (matches the asking price)
At profit margin = ~10% (industry average): company value ≈ $40M
Upside from industry-average improvement: $40M – $25M = $15M over purchase price
math.answer: $25M at 0% margin; ~$40M at industry-average margin of ~10%; $15M potential upside.

questions.prompt: What specific profit-improvement actions can PlasticWorld take, and how feasible are they?
questions.guidance: 1) Change sales force compensation from market-share-based to earnings/profit-based — easy to implement, directly removes the incentive to underprice. 2) Simplify the product line — PlasticWorld has 350 molds; eliminating less-used molds reduces material, tooling, and complexity costs. Must be done carefully given customer innovation pressures, but the superior sales force can manage customer relationships. 3) Examine industry best practices for additional cost or pricing improvements.

brainstorming.prompt: What other areas should the PE firm examine before or after the acquisition to further improve PlasticWorld's performance?

categories.name: Sales force & pricing
ideas: Implement price floor or minimum margin rules per account
Analyze customer price sensitivity to test upward pricing moves
Segment customers and tailor pricing by segment

categories.name: Product line rationalization
ideas: Audit all 350 molds for utilization and margin contribution
Standardize materials/finishes where customers are indifferent
Balance rationalization against customer-driven innovation needs

categories.name: Cost structure
ideas: Renegotiate supplier contracts with larger volume consolidation
Improve COGS efficiency through lean manufacturing
Review SG&A for redundant overhead after product line simplification
Evaluate whether depreciation asset base is fully utilized

categories.name: Customer strategy
ideas: Leverage customer loyalty to negotiate longer-term contracts at stable/higher prices
Co-develop innovation roadmap with key customers to justify premium pricing
Identify customer segments willing to pay for innovation vs. commodity

categories.name: Strategic positioning
ideas: Benchmark operations and pricing against the most profitable competitors
Explore adjacent markets or end-markets for the 350-mold capability
Assess whether any non-core assets can be divested post-acquisition

recommendation: Our client should accept the $25M offer and acquire PlasticWorld.
The company is currently worth ~$25M only if profitability is improved to break-even (0% margin); with identified changes it can reach ~$40M at industry-average margins — a $15M upside.
The highest-impact and easiest change is to immediately switch sales force compensation from market-share-based to earnings-based, eliminating the root cause of unnecessary price cuts.
Second priority is to rationalize the product line by eliminating underperforming molds from the 350-mold set to reduce costs, while using the strong sales force to maintain customer satisfaction.
risks: Sales force resistance or attrition if compensation change is poorly executed
Customer dissatisfaction if product line rationalization removes offerings customers value
Industry innovation pressures from customers may require continued R&D investment, limiting cost savings
Market share loss if price increases are not carefully managed
next_steps: Redesign sales force compensation plan tied to margin/profit before closing
Conduct detailed SKU profitability analysis across all 350 molds
Engage top customers to understand which product innovations are truly valued
Benchmark operational best practices against profitable industry peers
